specPoints.text: understand the concepts of food chains, food webs, pyramids of number, pyramids of biomass and pyramids of energy transfer

primer.text: Who eats whom decides where energy travels in an ecosystem. This note builds the diagram language: food chains with their producer-first rule, food webs that interweave many chains, and the three pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy that summarise each level in a drawing.

lessons.title: Food Chains
lessons.opening: A food chain is a diagram of who eats whom, with arrows that carry the energy from the first organism to the last, and every chain starts with a producer that can turn light into chemical energy.
keyPoints: Food chains show the flow of energy between organisms in an ecosystem.
Each arrow on a food chain diagram shows the transfer of energy between trophic levels.
Every food chain starts with a producer, such as a plant, that converts light energy into chemical energy.

low.restatement: A chain lists feeders in order, and the arrows show energy moving from lunch to diner.
low.analogy: A baton passed down a queue: each runner eats the one before and hands the energy on.
low.examPointer: Remember the double rule: arrows mean energy transfer, and the first organism is always a producer.

medium.restatement: The producer captures light energy into chemical energy, and each arrow then records energy flowing into the next trophic level as that organism feeds, which is why no chain can open with a consumer.
medium.analogy: A relay race that can only start when the first runner generates the baton from sunlight.
medium.examPointer: When reading or drawing chains, check the arrow points from eaten to eater — that is the energy direction.

check.stem: What do the arrows on a food chain diagram show?

options.text: The flow of energy between trophic levels
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The direction animals face while hunting
options.explanation: Arrows track energy, not gaze.

options.text: The movement of water through soil
options.explanation: Water is not what the arrows trace.

options.text: The age of each organism
options.explanation: Age plays no role in arrow direction.

check.stem: Why must every food chain begin with a producer?

options.text: Because producers convert light energy into chemical energy that other organisms can use
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because producers are the largest organisms
options.explanation: Size is not the reason; energy conversion is.

options.text: Because consumers cannot survive without sunlight directly
options.explanation: Consumers need food, not direct sunlight.

options.text: Because producers decay fastest
options.explanation: Decay speed is irrelevant to starting a chain.

check.stem: In the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle, which organism is the producer?

options.text: The grass
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The grasshopper, which eats first
options.explanation: Eating plants makes it a primary consumer, not a producer.

options.text: The frog, which sits mid-chain
options.explanation: Mid-chain predators are consumers.

options.text: The eagle at the top
options.explanation: Top predators are consumers, never the producer.

check.stem: Which direction does energy travel in the chain grass to vole to owl?

options.text: From grass to vole to owl, following the feeding steps
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: From owl to vole to grass
options.explanation: Energy flows from eaten to eater, not backwards.

options.text: From the air into every organism equally
options.explanation: Air does not feed the chain.

options.text: Back and forth between all three
options.explanation: Energy does not shuttle back and forth.

check.stem: A student draws an arrow from the eagle back to the grass in a food chain. Why is this wrong?

options.text: Energy cannot flow backwards because grass does not eat eagles
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Arrows must always point upwards on the page
options.explanation: Direction on the page is irrelevant; feeding direction matters.

options.text: The eagle is too large to arrow
options.explanation: Size does not block an arrow; diet does.

options.text: Arrows only belong in food webs
options.explanation: Food chains use arrows too.

check.stem: State what food chains show.
check.modelAnswer: Food chains show the flow of energy between organisms in an ecosystem through feeding.

check.stem: Name the kind of organism that every food chain starts with.
check.modelAnswer: Every food chain starts with a producer that converts light energy into chemical energy.

check.stem: Explain why a food chain cannot begin with a fox or a rabbit.
check.modelAnswer: A chain cannot begin with a fox or rabbit because neither converts light energy into chemical energy, so only a producer such as a plant can open the chain.

check.stem: A pond chain opens with algae followed by snails and then fish. Identify each role.
check.modelAnswer: Algae is the producer, snails are primary consumers feeding on it, and fish are secondary consumers eating the snails.

lessons.title: Food Webs
lessons.opening: Real ecosystems rarely feed in straight lines, so food webs weave many food chains together, letting one organism sit in several chains and take a different trophic level in each.
keyPoints: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains.
Food webs show the complexity of feeding relationships in an ecosystem.
One organism can occupy different trophic levels within the same web.
A change in one population, such as fewer rabbits, ripples through the other populations.

low.restatement: A web is many chains overlaid, so most animals hold several menu options.
low.analogy: A city map of bus routes: one stop connects to many lines, and closing one route shifts passengers everywhere.
low.examPointer: When a population changes, trace every chain it appears in before predicting effects.

medium.restatement: Because organisms feed on and are fed on by several partners, a web propagates change: fewer rabbits means less fox food, more uneaten grass, and shifts in every population linked to those chains, with populations rising or falling rather than vanishing.
medium.analogy: Dominoes standing in crossing rows — one topple travels down several lines at once.
medium.examPointer: Avoid writing die out; examiners want increases or decreases in population size.

check.stem: A food web is built from which structures within an ecosystem?

options.text: Many interconnected food chains
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: A single straight chain
options.explanation: One chain is not a web.

options.text: Circles of decomposers only
options.explanation: Webs include feeding at every level, not just decay.

options.text: Random arrows with no meaning
options.explanation: Every arrow in a web traces a feeding link.

check.stem: In a web, a fox eats rabbits and also eats mice. What does this show about the fox?

options.text: It occupies different feeding positions within the same web
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It must be a producer in one of the chains
options.explanation: Foxes never make their own food.

options.text: It can only hold one trophic level
options.explanation: Webs allow several levels for one organism.

options.text: It breaks the rules of a food web
options.explanation: Multiple links are exactly what webs allow.

check.stem: Rabbits decline sharply in a web where foxes also eat mice and frogs eat caterpillars. Which effect follows?

options.text: Foxes eat more of their other prey, pressuring those populations
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Foxes vanish at once
options.explanation: Decline is gradual; foxes switch prey first.

options.text: Grass disappears immediately
options.explanation: Less grazing usually lets grass increase.

options.text: Nothing changes anywhere
options.explanation: Webs propagate change; nothing stays isolated.

check.stem: Why do examiners prefer answers saying populations increase or decrease rather than die out?

options.text: Because partial links usually remain, so populations shift rather than vanish
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because extinction is illegal to write
options.explanation: It is a biological judgement, not a rule of law.

options.text: Because all animals are protected
options.explanation: Protection is not the reason; food alternatives are.

options.text: Because webs never change
options.explanation: Webs change constantly; the point is populations rarely hit zero.

check.stem: A web shows grass, caterpillars, earthworms, frogs, mice, rabbits, foxes and hawks. Rabbit numbers fall. What happens to the grass?

options.text: Grass growth increases because fewer rabbits feed on it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Grass declines with the rabbits
options.explanation: Less feeding means more grass, not less.

options.text: Grass stays frozen at the same amount
options.explanation: Released grazing pressure shifts growth upward.

options.text: Grass turns into a new species
options.explanation: Species do not transform in a web.

check.stem: State what food webs are made of.
check.modelAnswer: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains within an ecosystem.

check.stem: State one effect of a decrease in the rabbit population on the fox population in a food web.
check.modelAnswer: A decrease in rabbits reduces the food available to foxes, so the fox population decreases.

check.stem: Explain why one organism can hold several trophic levels in a food web.
check.modelAnswer: One organism holds several trophic levels because it feeds in different chains, acting as a secondary consumer in one and a tertiary consumer in another.

check.stem: In a web, caterpillars and earthworms increase after rabbits decline. Explain the link.
check.modelAnswer: With fewer rabbits, more grass survives, so caterpillars and earthworms gain extra plant food and their populations increase.

lessons.title: Pyramids of Numbers
lessons.opening: A pyramid of numbers simply counts heads at each trophic level, with bar width showing how many organisms live at that level, but the shape can surprise when many small creatures feed on one large one.
keyPoints: Pyramids of numbers display the count of organisms present at each trophic level.
The width of a bar tells you the number of organisms at that level.
When many small organisms feed on few large ones, the pyramid of numbers is not pyramid shaped.

low.restatement: Count the organisms at each level and draw a bar as wide as the count.
low.analogy: A seating chart: each row is as wide as the crowd sitting in it.
low.examPointer: Remember the exception: one huge producer like an oak tree can make the shape irregular.

medium.restatement: Because bars track raw counts, a single massive oak feeding thousands of caterpillars produces a narrow bar beneath a wide one, so pyramids of numbers can invert, unlike biomass or energy pyramids which measure amounts rather than heads.
medium.analogy: A census chart where one giant employer sits beside a thousand employees on the same row.
medium.examPointer: If a question shows an inverted bar diagram, check whether it plots numbers — the oak tree case is the classic.

check.stem: What does the width of a bar in a pyramid of numbers show?

options.text: The number of organisms at that trophic level
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The mass of living tissue
options.explanation: Mass belongs to biomass pyramids, not number pyramids.

options.text: The energy stored in each animal
options.explanation: Energy bars belong to energy pyramids.

options.text: The height each organism reaches
options.explanation: Physical height is never plotted.

check.stem: In the grass, vole, owl pyramid of numbers, which bar is narrowest?

options.text: The owl bar, because only one owl is counted
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The grass bar
options.explanation: Grass is numerous, so its bar is wide.

options.text: The vole bar
options.explanation: Voles outnumber owls in such a chain.

options.text: All bars match
options.explanation: Counts differ, so widths differ.

check.stem: Oak tree, caterpillar, robin, woodpecker — why can the pyramid of numbers look inverted?

options.text: Because one huge oak feeds many small caterpillars, so the counts rise along the chain
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because woodpeckers outnumber trees in nature
options.explanation: They do not; the oak is a single giant producer.

options.text: Because counting is always inaccurate
options.explanation: The shape reflects real counts, not error.

options.text: Because pyramids must invert by rule
options.explanation: No rule forces inversion; the sizes of organisms do.

check.stem: Which pyramid type can take any shape?

options.text: A pyramid of numbers
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: A pyramid of biomass
options.explanation: Biomass pyramids are always pyramid shaped.

options.text: A pyramid of energy
options.explanation: Energy pyramids are always pyramid shaped.

options.text: None, all pyramids match one shape
options.explanation: Numbers pyramids break the standard shape.

check.stem: Oak tree, caterpillar, robin, woodpecker — which pyramid of numbers statement is true?

options.text: The oak bar is narrowest because a single tree is counted
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The woodpecker bar is the widest
options.explanation: Top predators are fewest, so their bar is narrow.

options.text: All four bars match in width
options.explanation: Counts differ at every level, so widths differ.

options.text: The caterpillar bar is narrower than the oak bar
options.explanation: Many caterpillars feed on one oak, so their bar is wider.

check.stem: State what a pyramid of numbers displays.
check.modelAnswer: A pyramid of numbers displays the count of organisms living at each level of a food chain.

check.stem: State the shape of a pyramid of numbers when many small animals feed on one large tree.
check.modelAnswer: The pyramid of numbers is not pyramid shaped, because the count rises from one tree to many small feeders.

check.stem: Explain why the bar for one oak tree can be narrower than the caterpillar bar above it.
check.modelAnswer: The oak bar is narrow because a pyramid of numbers counts organisms, and a single large oak is just one organism while the caterpillars feeding on it are many.

check.stem: A daisy patch feeds hundreds of aphids, which feed a few ladybirds. Sketch the expected shape.
check.modelAnswer: The daisy bar is narrowest if counted as few plants, the aphid bar is widest, and the ladybird bar narrows again, giving an irregular shape rather than a clean pyramid.

lessons.title: Pyramids of Biomass & Energy
lessons.opening: Counting heads misleads when one organism outweighs a thousand others, so biomass pyramids weigh the living tissue at each level and energy pyramids measure the stored fuel, and both always narrow towards the top.
keyPoints: Pyramids of biomass display the mass of living organisms at every level of the chain.
Pyramids of biomass are always pyramid shaped because available biomass decreases at higher trophic levels.
Pyramids of energy record the stored energy held inside the biomass on every trophic level.
Pyramids of energy are also always pyramid shaped because energy is lost at each trophic level.
Bar width must match the unit measured, bars share the same height, and labels name each trophic level.

low.restatement: Weigh the living tissue or measure its stored fuel, and the bars always shrink towards the top.
low.analogy: A stack of parcels that gets lighter with every floor of the building.
low.examPointer: Drawing marks: labels on every bar, equal heights, width matching the unit, producers at the bottom.

medium.restatement: Biomass and energy both dwindle monotonically up a chain — less living tissue supports each next level and energy drains out at every step — so both pyramid types are always pyramid shaped, and drawing conventions lock producers at the bottom with equal-height labelled bars.
medium.analogy: A staircase of fuel tanks, each floor holding less than the one below, by physical necessity.
medium.examPointer: State the cause, not just the shape: biomass and energy decrease at each trophic level.

check.stem: What does a pyramid of biomass measure at each level?

options.text: The mass of living organisms present
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The count of individual animals
options.explanation: Counting is the job of a pyramid of numbers.

options.text: The energy trapped in sunlight
options.explanation: Sunlight energy is not plotted in biomass pyramids.

options.text: The area each species covers
options.explanation: Area covered is not a biomass measure.

check.stem: Why are pyramids of biomass always pyramid shaped?

options.text: Because available biomass always decreases towards higher trophic levels
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Because large animals always outnumber small ones
options.explanation: They usually do not; biomass still shrinks.

options.text: Because drawing conventions forbid other shapes
options.explanation: Convention follows reality; the decrease causes the shape.

options.text: Because producers weigh less than consumers
options.explanation: Producers carry the most biomass, not the least.

check.stem: What does a pyramid of energy record?

options.text: The stored energy held inside the biomass on every trophic level
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The total number of Joules in the Sun
options.explanation: Solar output is not plotted in these pyramids.

options.text: The mass of water in each organism
options.explanation: Water content is irrelevant here.

options.text: The speed of each animal
options.explanation: Speed is not a pyramid unit.

check.stem: Which two conventions apply when drawing any food pyramid?

options.text: Bars share the same height and each bar is labelled with its trophic level
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Bars grow taller at each level
options.explanation: Bar height stays constant; width carries the data.

options.text: Producers sit at the top
options.explanation: Producers always sit at the bottom.

options.text: Colour must match organism size
options.explanation: Colour is not part of the convention.

check.stem: Grass carries 10,000 units of energy and the wolf at the top carries 10. What explains the drop?

options.text: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so only a fraction reaches the next
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Wolves store energy more efficiently than grass
options.explanation: The loss between levels, not efficiency, causes the drop.

options.text: Energy disappears into the soil and never reappears
options.explanation: Energy leaves mainly as heat and waste, not soil storage.

options.text: Grass energy was measured wrongly
options.explanation: The pattern is real and expected, not a measurement error.

check.stem: State what biomass means.
check.modelAnswer: Biomass is the mass of living matter in the organisms at a trophic level.

check.stem: Name the two pyramid types that are always pyramid shaped.
check.modelAnswer: Pyramids of biomass and pyramids of energy are always pyramid shaped.

check.stem: Explain why a pyramid of energy can never invert, unlike a pyramid of numbers.
check.modelAnswer: A pyramid of energy can never invert because energy is lost at every feeding step, so each higher level must hold less stored energy than the level below it.

check.stem: A student draws an energy pyramid with a wider tertiary bar than the secondary bar. Correct it.
check.modelAnswer: The drawing is wrong because stored energy must fall at each step, so the tertiary bar must be narrower than the secondary bar beneath it.

glossary.definition: An organism that makes its own food, such as a plant converting light energy into chemical energy.
An organism that gains energy by feeding on other organisms.
A network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.
A bar diagram showing how many organisms are present at each trophic level.
The mass of living matter in the organisms at a trophic level.
